body.text: By all appearances, Myanmar junta leader Min Aung Hlaing has had a banner diplomatic year, chalking up a slew of high-profile visits to neighbouring states including China, India, Russia, Thailand, and Vietnam. In doing so, he has effectively outmanoeuvred the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), which did not recognise the results of the military’s fraudulent elections in January and which has barred high-level representatives from Myanmar from attending its summits.
Canberra needs to prepare for further rapid changes to Myanmar’s international status – rather than just react to first movers.

Now ASEAN appears to have lost control over the diplomatic process. In early October, Reuters revealed that the United States held secret talks with the Myanmar government in Tokyo in June, paving the way for a meeting between senior US officials and Min Aung Hlaing in Naypyidaw in September. According to Reuters, US Assistant Secretary of State for Intelligence and Research Michael Vance led the delegation’s visit to Naypyidaw with the ostensible aim of releasing detained American businessman Adam Castillo.

The visit served as convenient pretext for an engagement which the Trump administration had been mulling for some time. Ironically, Castillo had previously pitched the administration on potential access to Myanmar’s vast reserves of rare earths, which are critical to advanced technologies such as electric vehicles, solar panels, jet engines, and guided missiles. The problem is that Myanmar’s military does not control the territory where the rare earths lie, and China controls the supply chains of production.

Not to be outdone by recent US overtures to Naypyidaw, a Chinese delegation led by Peng Xiubin, director‑general of the Chinese Communist Party’s International Liaison Department, held a meeting in Myanmar in October with nine political parties, including the military’s proxy the Union Solidarity and Development Party (USDP) and eight other parties that the junta permitted to contest the 2025 election. Discussions focused on understanding public perception of China and strengthening the bilateral relationship.

Myanmar has been far from a priority in Washington since the 2021 military coup, which ended a decade of democratic reforms and saw the United States downgrade its diplomatic representation following Ambassador Thomas Vajda’s departure in 2022. But with the Trump administration’s openness to a new approach, great power competition is once again alive and well in Myanmar.

ASEAN has maintained that its Five Point Consensus is the preferred diplomatic path to resolve the crisis in Myanmar and bring Naypyidaw back into the fold. The plan, agreed in a special summit in 2021, calls for an end to violence, dialogue among all parties, mediation by a special envoy, humanitarian assistance, and a visit by that envoy to meet all parties. Philippine Secretary of Foreign Affairs Teresa Lazaro, the current special envoy for Myanmar, has insisted that Myanmar’s return to full participation in ASEAN’s meetings is “still far off.”
When Thailand takes up the ASEAN chairmanship in 2028, Bangkok is certain to advocate full normalisation of Myanmar’s membership.

But with Min Aung Hlaing’s recent spate of state visits to individual ASEAN member states, the bloc’s consensus-based position may be irrelevant. Indeed, the former general has travelled to five of the group’s 11 members this year alone, with reports that he may soon make trips to Indonesia and Brunei as well.

As regional leaders and great powers rush to shore up influence with the erstwhile pariah state, ASEAN finds itself in the uncomfortable position of being hung out to dry by its own members. The situation is particularly vexing for Singapore, which will take over the ASEAN chairmanship from the Philippines next month. Naturally, Singapore would rather focus on other pressing issues, such as setting the AI safety standards of the 21st century and advancing regional economic integration in the face of a shifting global order.

As chair, Singapore is likely to preserve the status quo for one more year, precluding Myanmar’s full participation in ASEAN for the time being. However, when Thailand takes up the chairmanship in 2028, Bangkok is certain to advocate full normalisation of Myanmar’s membership.

Canberra needs to prepare for further rapid changes to Myanmar’s international status – rather than just react to first movers. With Washington, Beijing, New Delhi and Moscow all courting Naypyidaw, and ASEAN’s leverage rapidly fading, Australian policymakers should consult regional partners and Washington to gauge where their Myanmar policies are heading.

At the same time, Canberra should be realistic about the likelihood of engagement bearing fruit. As long as Min Aung Hlaing and the generals are in power, we are unlikely to see meaningful reforms in Myanmar.
